Colorado Sheriffs Reject State's Gun Purchase Permit Requirement

Multiple Colorado sheriffs are refusing to issue the Firearms Safety Course Eligibility Card mandated by state law for purchases of AR-15s and other semi-automatic firearms. Montezuma County Sheriff Steven Nowlin leads a growing list of law enforcement officials declining to administer the permitting system, effectively blocking enforcement of Colorado's 2024 permit-to-purchase statute. The refusal exposes a critical weakness in state gun control measures: sheriffs' discretion to opt out.

Key Details

  • Colorado requires purchasers to complete a firearms safety course and obtain an eligibility card before buying AR-15s and many semi-automatic rifles
  • Montezuma County Sheriff Nowlin is not acting alone—additional sheriffs across Colorado are refusing to issue the cards
  • The opt-out strategy creates county-by-county enforcement gaps, making the statewide mandate effectively unenforceable in jurisdictions where sheriffs decline participation
  • No federal enforcement mechanism exists to compel state sheriffs to process state permits

Why It Matters for Gun Owners

Colorado gun owners in non-compliant counties now face a practical loophole. If your local sheriff refuses to issue eligibility cards, the permit-to-purchase requirement becomes a dead letter—you can legally purchase without the card because no authority is issuing it. This mirrors the successful nullification strategy used in other states where local law enforcement simply won't enforce state restrictions. Owners in compliant counties still face the burden: complete the course, wait for processing, and pay fees. The strategy also raises a larger question: can states actually mandate gun purchases through sheriffs' offices when those offices refuse?

DownRange Analysis

This is how Second Amendment pushback actually works at ground level. Colorado passed its permit-to-purchase law with confidence, but failed to account for constitutional sheriffs who view the mandate as unconstitutional infringement. The law depends entirely on voluntary sheriff compliance—there's no mechanism to override county-level refusal. Smart gun owners in opt-out counties should document their sheriff's non-compliance in writing and keep that record. In compliant counties, expect delays and fee structures designed to slow purchases. This won't survive a serious Bruen challenge if litigated, but Colorado may never get that far if sheriffs simply refuse to play.
